cards.explanation: The answer is False. The red heifer has to be unblemished with no defect, and it has never been placed under a yoke (Numbers 19:2). So that's a red heifer, a spotless one, and one that has never worked a day under a yoke. Finding that animal is a whole project, friends, and I bet the Israelites wanted it done right.

The answer is outside the camp. Eleazar the priest has the heifer brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence (Numbers 19:3). The whole thing happens out past the tents, friends. Nobody's doing this one in the middle of the neighborhood.

The answer is seven. Eleazar takes some of the blood on his finger and sprinkles it seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 19:4). Same finger, same direction, seven times in a row. That's a lot of sprinkling for one finger, bakers.

The answer is every part, including the hide and the dung. The text says its hide, its flesh and its blood are burned, along with its dung (Numbers 19:5). Nothing gets set aside for later, friends. The whole heifer goes into the fire.

The answer is cedar wood with hyssop and scarlet wool. The priest takes cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool and throws them onto the burning heifer (Numbers 19:6). Three things, one fire, bakers. That's the full list.

The answer is True. The priest washes his clothes and bathes, and he's still ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:7). The man who burned the heifer does the same and is unclean until evening too (Numbers 19:8). Washing is part of the job, friends, but the evening still has to come.

The answer is purification. The ashes are kept by the congregation of Israel for preparing the water of purification (Numbers 19:9). They aren't used up right away, bakers. A ceremonially clean man stores them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp until they're needed.

The answer is from sin. This water is for purification from sin (Numbers 19:9). Look at how the LORD sets it up, friends: a man who is ceremonially clean gathers the ashes and stores them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp, and the congregation of Israel keeps them for preparing the water. It's like setting aside one bowl of crushed peppermint for one batch and nothing else. That bowl has a job, and the verse names the job.

The answer is False. The man who gathered up the ashes must wash his clothes, and he will be ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:10). He started out clean, friends, and gathering the ashes changed that. Unlike the priest and the man who burned the heifer, this verse mentions only washing his clothes, not bathing (Numbers 19:7-8). Another load of laundry.

The answer is that he purifies himself with the water on the third and seventh days. For someone unclean from touching a dead body, the text says he must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and then he will be clean (Numbers 19:12). Both days count, bakers, so he can't skip the first one. Two days, one cleansing.

The answer is True. Anyone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself defiles the tabernacle of the LORD (Numbers 19:13). So skipping the water has a real cost, friends. His uncleanness stays on him.

The answer is that he must be cut off from Israel. Anyone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself must be cut off from Israel (Numbers 19:13). He remains unclean, bakers, because the water of purification has not been sprinkled on him. It's a serious one.

The answer is False. When someone dies in a tent, any open container without a lid fastened on it is unclean (Numbers 19:15). Fastened is the key word, friends. A lid sitting loose on top doesn't count, the way a cookie jar lid that's just resting there doesn't keep out a thing. So a lid that's really on is what matters in that tent.

The answer is touching a human bone or a grave. Anyone in the open field who touches a human bone or a grave will be unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). Same seven days as touching a body, bakers. Bones and graves count too.

The answer is fresh. Some of the ashes go into a jar, and fresh water is poured over them (Numbers 19:17). That's for the purification of the unclean person. Two ingredients, ashes and water, friends. Even I can handle a two-ingredient recipe, and I've scorched plenty of batches.

The answer is False. After the seventh day's sprinkling, the person must wash his clothes and bathe in water, and that evening he will be clean (Numbers 19:19). So there's still laundry and a bath between the sprinkling and the finish, bakers. Clean comes that evening, not right after the sprinkling.

The answer is unclean! Anything the unclean person touches becomes unclean (Numbers 19:22). And it doesn't stop there, friends, because whoever touches that thing is unclean until evening. Picture a thumb covered in chocolate. It grabs the cookie box, the box is smeared, and the next hand that picks it up is smeared too.
